title: JESUS SAID IT WOULD HAVE BEEN BETTER IF JUDAS HAD NEVER BEEN BORN. WHAT DID HE KNOW THAT SHOULD TERRIFY US TODAY?
paragraphs: JESUS SAID IT WOULD HAVE BEEN BETTER IF JUDAS HAD NEVER BEEN BORN. WHAT DID HE KNOW THAT SHOULD TERRIFY US TODAY?

He walked with Jesus, witnessed miracles, heard the truth from the mouth of God Himself—and still betrayed Him. But the most frightening part of Judas' story isn't the thirty pieces of silver. It's what Jesus said about the man who would betray Him.
There is a sentence in the Bible so devastating that it should make even the most confident Christian stop and examine their heart.
It wasn't spoken to a demon.
It wasn't spoken to a Roman executioner.
It wasn't spoken to someone who had spent his entire life openly rejecting God.
It was spoken about a man who had walked beside Jesus.
A man who had eaten with Him, traveled with Him, listened to His teachings, and watched Him perform miracles that most people could only dream of witnessing.
His name was Judas Iscariot.
And on the night before His crucifixion, Jesus said something almost unbearable.
"The Son of man goeth as it is written of him: but woe unto that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed! it had been good for that man if he had not been born." — Matthew 26:24, KJV
Read that last sentence again.
It would have been better for that man if he had never been born.
What kind of spiritual tragedy could make the Savior of the world speak such words?
What did Judas lose that made his very existence something Jesus could describe this way?
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question of all...
Could someone spend years close to Christianity, become familiar with the language of faith, participate in ministry, and still never truly surrender to Christ?
Because the story of Judas is not merely about a traitor who lived two thousand years ago.
It is also a warning about the frightening distance that can exist between being near Jesus and actually belonging to Him.
And before this story ends, there is something we must understand about Judas, repentance, and the mercy of Christ that may change the way we look at our own souls.
Judas was not an outsider looking through the window.
He was inside the room.
When Jesus called His twelve apostles, Judas was among them. Scripture tells us that Jesus appointed the Twelve to be with Him and to be sent out to preach (Mark 3:13–19).
Think about what that means.
Judas lived in extraordinary proximity to the incarnate Son of God.
He heard Jesus teach about forgiveness.
He watched Him welcome sinners.
He witnessed the compassion of Christ toward the broken, the rejected, and the spiritually lost.
When Jesus spoke about the kingdom of heaven, Judas was there.
When Jesus warned about hypocrisy, Judas was there.
When Jesus taught that no one could serve both God and money, Judas was there.
And still, somewhere beneath the outward appearance of discipleship, something was terribly wrong.
John's Gospel gives us a disturbing glimpse into his character.
Judas was entrusted with the disciples' moneybag, but John 12:6 says he was a thief who used to take what was put into it.
That detail matters.
The betrayal did not appear in the biblical narrative as one isolated moment disconnected from everything that came before.
Scripture reveals an existing pattern of dishonesty.
Judas had access to sacred things while secretly misusing what had been entrusted to him.
He could stand beside Jesus while stealing from the common purse.
He could hear the truth while nurturing a hidden sin.
He could look like a disciple while his heart remained dangerously divided.
And that should unsettle us.
Because it is possible to know the right Christian vocabulary while refusing to obey the Christ we speak about.
It is possible to serve in a church while privately feeding an addiction to approval, money, lust, resentment, or power.
It is possible to defend biblical truth in public while making peace with deliberate disobedience in private.
Not every struggling Christian is a Judas. Every believer battles sin and needs grace.
But there is a difference between fighting sin with a repentant heart and protecting sin while pretending nothing is wrong.
Judas forces us to confront that difference.
And then came the night that changed history.
Matthew 26 tells us that Judas went to the chief priests and asked what they would give him to deliver Jesus into their hands.
They weighed out thirty pieces of silver.
The Gospel does not tell us every thought that passed through Judas' mind. We should not pretend to know what Scripture has not revealed.
But it does tell us what he did.
He agreed to betray Jesus.
And from that moment, he sought an opportunity.
Imagine the terrible contradiction.
While Jesus moved toward the cross to give His life for sinners, one of His own apostles was looking for the right moment to hand Him over.
The Savior was preparing to shed His blood.
The betrayer had accepted silver.
And then they gathered for the Passover meal.
Jesus sat with the Twelve.
The atmosphere was intimate. The hour was solemn.
These were men who had shared the road with Him, endured opposition, and listened to His words.
Then Jesus announced:
"Verily I say unto you, that one of you shall betray me." — Matthew 26:21, KJV
The disciples were deeply sorrowful.
One after another, they asked, "Lord, is it I?"
And Judas also asked.
"Master, is it I?" — Matthew 26:25, KJV
Jesus answered him:
"Thou hast said."
There is something almost unbearable about that exchange.
Judas could still speak to Jesus.
He could still sit at the table.
He could still participate in the meal.
But his outward nearness concealed an inward betrayal.
And this is where Jesus pronounced the warning that echoes through the centuries.
"It had been good for that man if he had not been born."
To understand the weight of those words, we need to examine what Matthew actually recorded.
The New Testament was written in Koine Greek, and the crucial expression in Matthew 26:24 reads:
καλὸν ἦν αὐτῷ εἰ οὐκ ἐγεννήθη ὁ ἄνθρωπος ἐκεῖνος
kalon ēn autō ei ouk egennēthē ho anthrōpos ekeinos
A faithful rendering is:
"It would have been better for that man if he had not been born."
The Greek word καλόν (kalon) can convey what is good, fitting, or preferable.
Here, in context, Jesus is not making a casual statement about the difficulties of life.
He is expressing the horrifying seriousness of the judgment awaiting His betrayer.
And the warning immediately preceding it begins with another important Greek word:
οὐαί (ouai) — "woe."
In biblical usage, "woe" can express lament, denunciation, or the announcement of judgment, depending on the context.
Here it carries a grave warning.
Jesus was not merely saying that Judas had made an unfortunate career decision or committed a mistake he would someday regret.
He was announcing the dreadful moral and spiritual weight of betraying the Son of Man.
And there is another detail we cannot afford to overlook.
Jesus said:
"The Son of man goeth as it is written of him..."
In other words, His coming suffering was not an unexpected defeat.
The betrayal and crucifixion did not catch God by surprise.
The Scriptures had already testified to the suffering of the Messiah.
Yet Jesus immediately added:
"But woe unto that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed!"
Do you see the tension?
God's redemptive purpose was being fulfilled.
And Judas was still responsible for his actions.
Divine sovereignty did not erase human accountability.
The fact that God would bring salvation through the cross did not make Judas' betrayal righteous.
God can accomplish His holy purposes even through wicked human actions without becoming the author or approver of that wickedness.
Acts 2:23 makes the same truth clear when Peter speaks of Jesus being delivered according to God's determined purpose and foreknowledge, while holding those who crucified Him responsible.
The cross was God's saving plan.
The betrayal was still evil.
And the warning was still real.
But now we must ask the question that troubles so many readers.
Did Jesus mean that Judas was condemned forever?
The language of Matthew 26:24 is extraordinarily severe.
If never having been born would be preferable to what awaited Judas, Jesus was describing a consequence of terrifying magnitude.
The immediate context is divine judgment, not merely embarrassment, earthly suffering, or the loss of a friendship.
Other passages deepen the warning.
In John 17:12, Jesus refers to the one who was lost as "the son of perdition" in the KJV.
The Greek expression is ὁ υἱὸς τῆς ἀπωλείας (ho huios tēs apōleias), meaning "the son of destruction" or "the son of perdition."
The expression describes someone characterized by or destined for destruction.
In John 6:70, Jesus also says that one of the Twelve is a devil, and John identifies Judas as the one in view.
Taken together, these passages give grave biblical grounds for understanding Judas' end as one of destruction and judgment.
But we must be careful.
Scripture does not invite us to invent details about Judas' experience after death, nor does it give us permission to pronounce the eternal destiny of every person who has committed a terrible sin.
Jesus' warning is severe enough without adding claims the text does not make.
And it is not a declaration that every person who betrays trust, falls into sin, or experiences spiritual collapse is beyond the mercy of God.
That distinction matters more than we may realize.
Because someone reading this may already be thinking:
"I betrayed Jesus too."
Maybe you once promised you would never return to a certain sin.
And you returned.
Maybe you knew what was right and deliberately chose what was wrong.
Maybe you hurt people who trusted you.
Maybe you once served God passionately, but now you hardly recognize the person you have become.
And when you read about Judas, something inside you whispers:
"What if I've gone too far?"
Listen carefully.
The story of Judas is a warning against refusing Christ, not permission to despair of Christ's mercy.
And the difference becomes even clearer when we place Judas beside another disciple.
Peter.
On the same night Jesus was betrayed, Peter made a bold promise.
He insisted that even if others fell away, he would remain faithful.
Yet before the rooster crowed, Peter denied Jesus three times.
He denied knowing the very Savior he had promised to follow.
And when the rooster crowed, Peter remembered the words of Jesus.
Matthew 26:75 tells us that he went out and wept bitterly.
Now consider Judas.
After Jesus was condemned, Matthew 27:3 tells us that Judas regretted what he had done.
He returned the thirty pieces of silver and confessed:
"I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood." — Matthew 27:4, KJV
That confession was true.
Jesus was innocent.
Judas had sinned.
The money had not been worth it.
But returning the silver could not undo the betrayal.
And the chief priests offered him no comfort.
"What is that to us? see thou to that."
Judas threw down the silver in the temple, departed, and took his own life.
It is one of the darkest endings recorded in the Gospels.
And we must approach it with both theological seriousness and human compassion.
Matthew uses the Greek verb μεταμεληθείς (metamelētheis) to describe Judas' regret in Matthew 27:3.
The word conveys regret or a change of feeling or concern.
It is different from μετάνοια (metanoia), the noun commonly associated with repentance—a turning of mind and heart toward God.
That difference is meaningful, but it should not be exaggerated into a simplistic rule that one Greek word always means worldly remorse and the other always guarantees saving repentance.
Biblical words must be understood in context.
What the narrative actually shows is that Judas acknowledged his guilt, attempted to return the money, and then fell into a tragic end.
It does not show him returning to Jesus in faith.
Peter, by contrast, was restored by the risen Christ.
In John 21, Jesus asked Peter three times whether he loved Him, and commissioned him to care for His sheep.
Two disciples.
Two terrible failures.
Two very different recorded endings.
And the difference is not that Peter's sin was harmless or that Peter possessed some natural superiority.
Peter needed grace just as desperately as Judas.
The difference we can clearly see in Scripture is that Peter's story continued into restoration through Jesus Christ.
This is where the Gospel begins to shine through the darkness.
Because the good news is not that real Christians never fail.
The good news is that Jesus Christ saves sinners who cannot save themselves.
Peter was not restored because his tears purchased forgiveness.
He was restored by the Savior he had denied.
And if you are still breathing, still hearing the call of the Gospel, still being confronted by the truth of God's Word, do not turn your conviction into an excuse to run farther away.
Come to Christ.
Not because your sin is small.
But because His mercy is greater than anything you could ever earn.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
That promise is not an invitation to treat sin lightly.
It is an invitation to bring sin into the light.
And Jesus Himself said:
"...him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." — John 6:37, KJV
That is the voice a repentant sinner needs to hear.
Not the voice of denial.
Not the voice of self-justification.
Not the voice that says sin doesn't matter.
But the voice of the Savior who receives those who come to Him.
And perhaps this is the most heartbreaking aspect of Judas' story.
He had spent years near the One who came to seek and save the lost.
Yet his recorded story ends in ruin.
We must not pretend to know everything that passed through Judas' mind in his final hours. Scripture does not reveal that.
But it shows us enough to ask a question that cuts deeper than most religious conversations ever reach.
What good is being close to the things of God if we refuse to give our hearts to God Himself?
You can own several Bibles and never submit to the truth inside them.
You can attend worship every week and still live a secret life of deliberate rebellion.
You can quote Scripture to correct others while refusing to let Scripture correct you.
You can build a reputation around Christianity while neglecting the Christ whose name you carry.
You can even become so comfortable around sacred things that you stop trembling at the possibility of dishonoring the One who is holy.
And the danger is not that struggling believers occasionally fall.
The danger is learning to live comfortably with a divided heart.
A heart that wants the benefits of Jesus without His authority.
A heart that wants forgiveness without repentance.
A heart that wants heaven without surrender.
A heart that wants the appearance of discipleship without the reality of following Christ.
Jesus warned in Matthew 7:21 that not everyone who calls Him "Lord, Lord" will enter the kingdom of heaven.
That warning should never be used to terrorize tender consciences or convince genuinely repentant believers that salvation depends on achieving sinless perfection.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not by works (Ephesians 2:8–9).
But the grace that saves us does not leave us indifferent to the One who saved us.
Ephesians 2:10 goes on to say that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
True faith is not a flawless performance.
It is a living trust in the real Jesus that bears fruit by His grace.
And Judas reminds us that religious proximity is not the same thing as saving faith.
But there is something else in the betrayal narrative that makes the Gospel even more astonishing.
Jesus knew.
He knew what Judas was going to do.
He was not fooled by a convincing smile.
He was not surprised by a hidden agreement.
He was not helplessly stumbling toward an unforeseen catastrophe.
John 13:11 explicitly says that Jesus knew who would betray Him.
And still, the Son of God continued toward the cross.
Not because evil had defeated Him.
But because He had come to accomplish the salvation of sinners.
Think about that.
The very night that exposed the depths of human betrayal also moved the world toward the greatest revelation of divine love.
At the cross, human wickedness was displayed in horrifying clarity.
And at the cross, God's saving grace was revealed in breathtaking power.
Jesus did not die because humanity was secretly good enough to deserve Him.
He died for sinners.
Romans 5:8 says:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had repaired every broken relationship.
Not after we had conquered every temptation.
Not after we had accumulated enough religious achievements to impress heaven.
Christ died for us while we were sinners.
And His resurrection declares that death did not have the final word.
This is why the answer to spiritual failure is not to become better at pretending.
It is to come honestly to the crucified and risen Christ.
The Gospel does not say, "Hide your scandal until you look worthy of grace."
It says that Jesus came to save the lost.
The Gospel does not erase the seriousness of sin.
It reveals the Savior who bore sin's judgment for those who belong to Him.
And that is why our message at Gospel Warrior is more than a beautiful phrase.
Not because every story automatically receives the ending we want.
Not because repentance is unnecessary.
Not because grace makes disobedience harmless.
But because the living Christ has the power to forgive, reconcile, restore, and transform those who turn to Him in faith.
The cross is where the sinner's hope begins.
The resurrection is why that hope is not empty.
And the call to repentance is not God's cruelty.
It is His mercy confronting us before we become comfortable with destruction.
Perhaps you have been living a double life.
Perhaps no one knows what you have been carrying.
Perhaps your family sees the strong Christian, your church sees the dependable servant, and your friends see the person who always seems to have the right answers.
But God sees the nights you struggle.
The compromises you justify.
The prayers you have stopped praying.
The bitterness you have refused to release.
The truth you keep avoiding.
And maybe this article has reached the part of your heart you have been trying to protect from conviction.
Do not waste that moment.
You do not have to perform holiness for God.
You need to come before Him honestly.
Confess what you have been hiding.
Turn away from what is destroying you.
Trust the Savior who died and rose again.
And if you need help, reach out to a mature Christian, a faithful pastor, or someone who can walk beside you with biblical wisdom and compassion.
There is no shame in needing discipleship.
There is danger in pretending you do not need grace.

And if you have fallen so far that you are beginning to believe your life is beyond repair, please hear this too: Judas' death is not an example to imitate. Despair is not repentance, and taking your own life is not a way to make things right. If you are thinking of harming yourself, tell someone you trust immediately and seek urgent help. Your life matters, and help is available.
The right response to the warning of Judas is not self-destruction.
It is to seek life in Jesus Christ.
Now return to the words that began this story.
"It had been good for that man if he had not been born."
Jesus was not teaching that life itself is worthless.
Human life is a gift from God.
Nor was He declaring that every person who has committed a devastating betrayal must share Judas' fate.
He was pronouncing a uniquely severe warning concerning the man who would betray Him.
And the warning remains a sobering reminder that spiritual choices have eternal significance.
We cannot purchase salvation.
We cannot earn it through religious performance.
We cannot inherit it merely by being surrounded by Christian people.
And we cannot replace a personal response to Jesus with familiarity about Jesus.
The question is not simply whether we know His name.
It is whether we have come to Him in repentance and faith.
Because there is a world of difference between carrying a Bible and being changed by the Word of God.
Between knowing Christian songs and worshiping Christ in spirit and truth.
Between wearing a cross and trusting the Savior who died upon one.
Between admiring Jesus and following Him.
And there is a world of difference between regretting the consequences of sin and turning to the Lord for mercy.
Not to embarrass you.
Not to make you feel spiritually inferior.
But because some questions are too important to avoid.
If Jesus exposed the hidden condition of your heart today, what would He find?
A believer who is struggling but still turning to Him?
A wounded soul who desperately needs healing?
Someone who has been pretending to be spiritually healthy?
Someone who has been postponing repentance because tomorrow always seems guaranteed?
Or someone who has never truly placed their trust in Christ?
Whatever the answer, do not answer with another performance.
Answer with honesty before God.
You can begin with a simple prayer.

"Lord Jesus, You know everything about me. You know my sins, my fears, my compromises, and the things I have hidden from others. I cannot save myself. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Have mercy on me. Forgive me, turn my heart away from sin, and teach me to follow You in truth. I do not want merely to appear close to You. I want to belong to You. In Your name, amen."
And if that prayer expresses the genuine desire of your heart, do not let this moment end with emotion alone.
Open the Scriptures.
Seek fellowship with faithful believers.
Ask for prayer.
Take the next obedient step.
And keep looking to Christ.
Because the goal of this article is not to make you fascinated with Judas.
It is to make you see Jesus more clearly.
The Jesus who spoke truth even when that truth was terrifying.
The Jesus who never treated sin as something insignificant.
The Jesus who went willingly to the cross.
The Jesus who rose from the grave.
The Jesus who restores repentant sinners and calls His people to follow Him.
And now I want to ask something of you.
Someone reading silently may need to know that repentance, grace, and a new beginning are real.
Your words might become the encouragement another believer needs to keep seeking Jesus.

Not simply to increase the number of people who see it, but because someone among your friends may be outwardly smiling while privately struggling with guilt, spiritual exhaustion, or the fear that God could never forgive them.
But I also want to speak to those who believe that the message of Jesus Christ deserves to reach farther.
Gospel Warrior is committed to making biblical teaching and discipleship resources accessible to people who are hungry for the Word of God.
We want people to have access to resources that encourage prayer, strengthen biblical understanding, confront spiritual compromise, and point readers toward the Savior.
And continuing and expanding that work requires faithful support.
The New Testament teaches that Christian giving should be willing, sincere, and free from pressure.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver."
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not out of guilt.
Not because God needs your money.
But because freely supporting trustworthy Gospel work can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership in ministry.
You can glorify God through prayer, faithful obedience, loving service, sharing His Word, and generous giving according to your ability and conviction.
Those items are simply gifts and resources connected to the ministry. They are not the Gospel itself.
Jesus Christ is the treasure.
The Word of God is the nourishment.
And spiritual growth is the purpose.
Keep reading.
Keep growing.
Keep praying.
Keep sharing the truth.
Your worth before God is not measured by a monthly payment, and the free resources are intended to remain a blessing to those who need them.
One sincere prayer, one thoughtful comment, one article shared with a struggling friend, or one honest conversation about Jesus can become part of something deeply meaningful.
The Gospel is not merchandise.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
That is the message worth carrying into the world.
And that brings us back to Judas.
Thirty pieces of silver.
One terrible betrayal.
One devastating warning.
And a question that reaches across two thousand years into the quiet places of our hearts.
What are we allowing to compete with our devotion to Jesus?
What secret compromise have we been calling harmless?
What part of our lives have we refused to surrender?
And how long will we keep assuming there will always be another opportunity to turn back?
Judas reminds us that spiritual privilege is not the same as spiritual life.
Peter reminds us that devastating failure need not be the end of a disciple's story.
But Jesus is the One who gives both stories their deepest significance.
He is the holy Savior who warns us about judgment.
He is the crucified Redeemer who offers forgiveness.
He is the risen Lord who calls sinners to repent and believe.
And He is worthy of more than a religious appearance.
He is worthy of our trust, our love, our obedience, and our lives.
So do not leave this story merely afraid of becoming like Judas.
Leave it determined to come to Jesus.
Not tomorrow.
Not when you have cleaned yourself up.
Not when you finally feel worthy.
Come to Him in faith, with an honest heart, and receive the grace that no amount of silver could ever buy.
Judas stood close enough to Jesus to kiss His face, yet his story warns us that the most tragic distance from Christ can be the distance hidden inside the human heart.
